topic: Earworms: why a song gets stuck in your head
title: Why That Song Won't Leave Your Head
voiceover: Why is that song stuck in your head? Scientists call it involuntary musical imagery, or an earworm. In a survey of 12,519 Finnish adults, 89 percent reported having one at least once a week. A 2016 study compared tunes that people named as earworms with other songs. Earworm tunes tended to have faster tempos. They also followed common melodic shapes, with unusual steps between turning points. In 2015, Beaman and colleagues had 98 people try not to think about two pop songs for three minutes. People chewing gum reported hearing the songs less often than people who did nothing or tapped their fingers. The authors suggest gum interferes with the motor planning behind imagining the song. So chewing gum might help next time, though this was a small lab experiment. Tomorrow: can a random number change your guess?

description: Why does a song get stuck in your head? A large survey found nearly nine in ten people get an earworm weekly, earworm tunes tend to be faster with common melodic shapes, and chewing gum reduced them in a small lab experiment. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Beaman, C. P., Powell, K., & Rapley, E. (2015). Want to block earworms from conscious awareness? B(u)y gum!. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 68(6), 1049-1057. Source: Liikkanen, L. A. (2012). Musical activities predispose to involuntary musical imagery. Psychology of Music, 40(2), 236-256.
accuracy_note: Survey figure (89.2% weekly, N=12,519) is from Finnish internet users and may not generalize. The gum result is from small lab experiments (Experiment 1: 98 people) and is not a guaranteed cure. Jakubowski et al. compared tunes named as earworms with other songs; it describes tendencies, not rules.
